candidates.snippet:
run: |
          curl -X POST "https://api.vercel.com/v1/deployments" \
            -H "Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }}" \
            -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
            -d "{\"name\": \"nomadhome\", \"project\": \"${{ secrets.VERCEL_PROJECT_ID }}\", \"deploymentDataSource\": \"github\"}"

findings.title: Secrets interpolated directly into a run-step shell command
findings.description: `VERCEL_TOKEN` (L19) and `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID` (L21) are inlined into the `run:` curl command via `${{ secrets.* }}`, which renders the secret values into the shell command string at expansion time. GitHub's own guidance discourages this in favor of passing secrets through `env:` and referencing `$VAR`, because inline expansion widens the surface for accidental log/command-line exposure and for shell breakage/injection if a value ever contained metacharacters. Practical exploitability is low: this workflow triggers only on `push` to `main` (trusted committers, no untrusted PR input), the secrets are admin-set and masked in logs, and Vercel IDs/tokens are not attacker-controlled. Reported as a best-practice hardening item.
findings.recommendation: Move the secrets into an `env:` block on the step and reference them as environment variables in the curl command (e.g. `env: { VERCEL_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }} }` then `-H "Authorization: Bearer $VERCEL_TOKEN"`), quoting expansions to avoid word-splitting.
